## No tutor again — specific risks for Day 3

Mixed-effects models produce confusing output and cryptic errors
(convergence failures, singular fits, boundary issues). Debugging
individual models with 35 students is impossible. Design decisions
baked in:

- Specific, pre-tested model formulas — don't let students invent
  their own in §2 or §3
- The `performance` package for diagnostics (one function, nice output)
  rather than base R residual plots
- Framing throughout: "this is a tool you'll keep learning for years"
  — don't try to teach everything today
:::

## 09:10–10:00 · §1. Refresher — stats and regression concepts (50 min)

**Aim.** Every student can read an `lm()` output: identify the intercept,
coefficients, standard errors, p-values, and R². Know what a coefficient
means (not just how to find one).

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 7 (`07-statistics.qmd`).

### 1.1 Intro (15 min)

Key points — these are the concepts you'll lean on all day:

- **Descriptive statistics** describe your sample. **Inferential
  statistics** let you generalise from your sample to a population.
- **A regression model** describes how one variable (outcome) depends
  on one or more others (predictors). Linear regression predicts a
  continuous outcome; logistic regression predicts a binary one.
- **Coefficients** = the regression equation. For `lm(y ~ x)`:
  - Intercept = predicted y when x = 0
  - Slope of x = change in y per unit change in x
- **Standard error** = uncertainty around the coefficient
- **p-value** = probability of seeing a coefficient this large (or
  larger) if the true coefficient were zero. Small p = evidence
  against "no effect".
- **R²** = proportion of variance in y explained by the model. Not a
  measure of being "right" — a measure of fit.

Don't:

- Define *null hypothesis* formally (you'll lose the room)
- Talk about assumptions (homoscedasticity, independence) — covered when needed
- Introduce t-tests and chi-square separately (regression subsumes them)

### 1.2 Students try (10 min)

> Fit a quick linear model to a built-in R dataset:
>
> ```r
> # Built-in dataset: 32 cars, miles-per-gallon vs weight
> head(mtcars)
>
> # Fit: mpg as a function of weight
> m1 <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
> summary(m1)
> ```
>
> Look at the output. Can you say in one sentence what the model shows?

Walk the room briefly. Help students read the summary — point at the
coefficient estimate, SE, p-value, R² at the bottom.

### 1.3 Demo (15 min)

Build intuition — plot the model, add a second predictor, show how
coefficients change:

```{r demo-1-3, eval=TRUE}
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)

# The simple model
m1 <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
summary(m1)

# Tidy output
broom::tidy(m1)
broom::glance(m1)

# Visualise
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "Miles per gallon",
       title = "mpg ~ wt") +
  theme_bw()

# Add a second predictor
m2 <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
summary(m2)

# Compare: how did the wt coefficient change?
broom::tidy(m1)
broom::tidy(m2)

# What about a categorical predictor?
mtcars$cyl_f <- factor(mtcars$cyl)
m3 <- lm(mpg ~ wt + cyl_f, data = mtcars)
summary(m3)
```

Talking points:

- Each coefficient is "the effect of this predictor **holding others
  constant**"
- Adding predictors changes the coefficients of ones already there —
  this is why *controlling for* matters
- Categorical predictors: R picks a reference level, each other level
  is a coefficient saying how far it is from the reference
- `broom::tidy()` gives you the coefficients as a tibble — nice for
  reporting

No exercise — this is a refresher. §2 is where application starts.

## 10:15–12:00 · §2. Linear mixed-effects models (105 min)

**Aim.** Every student fits a linear mixed-effects model, interprets
the fixed effects, and understands why random intercepts are needed.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 8 (`08-mixed-effects-models.qmd`).

::: {.callout-note}
## Dataset: `sleepstudy` from the `lme4` package

`sleepstudy` is a built-in dataset: 18 subjects, each measured for 10
days of sleep deprivation, with reaction time as the outcome. It's the
canonical teaching example for `lmer`. No file to load — just
`library(lme4)`.
:::

### 2.1 Intro (20 min)

Key points — take time here, the concepts matter:

- **The problem.** Most real data is grouped. Subjects produce multiple
  tokens. Speakers come from multiple corpora. Students belong to
  multiple schools. If you fit a plain `lm()` on grouped data, you
  violate independence of observations — one of the fundamental
  assumptions.
- **Treating subject as a fixed effect** (one dummy per subject) uses
  up degrees of freedom and doesn't let you generalise beyond the
  specific subjects you have.
- **The mixed-effects solution.** Treat subject as a **random effect**:
  model each subject as drawn from a population of subjects. You
  estimate the *variability* among subjects, not each subject's
  intercept individually. Fewer parameters, generalisable results.
- **Random intercepts.** Each subject gets their own baseline. All
  subjects share the same slope for predictors.
- **Random slopes.** Each subject gets their own baseline AND their
  own slope for a predictor. Allows the effect of a predictor to
  vary across subjects.
- **The notation.** `(1 | Subject)` = random intercept for Subject.
  `(1 + Days | Subject)` = random intercept AND random slope for Days
  by Subject. The `1` is the intercept; `Days` is the predictor whose
  slope varies.

Draw on the whiteboard:

1. A scatter plot of outcome vs predictor, with points coloured by subject
2. A single regression line through all points (= plain `lm()`)
3. Parallel lines, one per subject (= random intercepts)
4. Non-parallel lines, one per subject (= random intercepts + slopes)

This diagram is more useful than any formula.

### 2.2 Students try (20 min)

> With `library(lme4)` loaded:
>
> ```r
> library(lme4)
> library(lmerTest)   # adds p-values to lmer output
>
> # Inspect the data
> head(sleepstudy)
> summary(sleepstudy)
>
> # Simplest: ignore the grouping (WRONG but useful to see)
> m0 <- lm(Reaction ~ Days, data = sleepstudy)
> summary(m0)
>
> # Add random intercept by Subject
> m1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
> summary(m1)
> ```
>
> Compare the Days coefficient in `m0` and `m1`. Did it change?
>
> Then look at the "Random effects" section of the lmer output. What's
> the standard deviation of the Subject intercept?

Walk the room, point at the "Random effects" block — it's the key
thing that distinguishes `lmer` from `lm` output.

### 2.3 Demo (35 min)

Build up to a model with random intercepts AND slopes:

```{r demo-2-3, eval=TRUE}
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(ggplot2)
library(performance)
library(sjPlot)

# Random intercept only
m1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
summary(m1)

# Random intercept AND slope
m2 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
summary(m2)

# What changed?
#  - Random effects block now has 2 variances + 1 correlation
#  - Fixed effects estimates are similar
#  - Model has more parameters → compare with AIC

anova(m1, m2)  # likelihood ratio test
AIC(m1, m2)    # information criterion comparison

# Visualise individual subject lines
ggplot(sleepstudy, aes(x = Days, y = Reaction, group = Subject)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(stat = "smooth", method = "lm", se = FALSE,
            alpha = 0.4, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm",
              se = FALSE, colour = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Individual subject slopes (blue) vs population slope (red)",
       x = "Days of sleep deprivation",
       y = "Reaction time (ms)") +
  theme_bw()

# Diagnostics — one line with performance
performance::check_model(m2)

# Model summary table for publication
sjPlot::tab_model(m2)

# R² (marginal = fixed only; conditional = fixed + random)
performance::r2(m2)
```

Talking points:

- The Days coefficient (~10 ms/day) is the main finding — reaction
  time slows by ~10 ms per day of sleep deprivation
- The random slope variance tells you subjects differ in how fast
  they slow down — not just WHERE they start
- `anova(m1, m2)` is a likelihood ratio test — formally compares
  nested models
- `performance::check_model()` gives you ALL the diagnostics in one
  call — residuals, normality, collinearity, outliers
- `sjPlot::tab_model()` gives you a publication-ready summary table

### 2.4 Exercise (30 min)

> **Task.** Still using `sleepstudy`:
>
> 1. Fit a model with ONLY a random intercept for Subject (`m1`
>    from the demo)
> 2. Fit a model with random intercept AND random slope for Days
>    (`m2` from the demo)
> 3. Compare them with `anova(m1, m2)` — which is preferred?
> 4. For the winning model: report the Days coefficient with its SE
>    and p-value in one sentence of plain English
> 5. Produce `performance::check_model()` output. Flag any assumption
>    that looks violated
> 6. Produce `sjPlot::tab_model(m2)` — save the HTML
>
> Commit everything to `day3.R`.
>
> **Stretch:** add a quadratic term for Days (`Days + I(Days^2)`). Does
> the model prefer it over a linear fit?

Common failure modes:

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `boundary (singular) fit` | Random slope variance ~0 | Model is overspecified — drop random slope |
| `Model failed to converge` | Not enough data / too complex | Simplify random structure |
| p-values missing from summary | Didn't load `lmerTest` | `library(lmerTest)` then refit |

## 13:00–14:15 · §3. Logistic mixed-effects models (75 min)

**Aim.** Every student fits a logistic mixed-effects model, interprets
the output (log-odds vs probabilities), and understands when logistic
vs linear is appropriate.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 8 (`08-mixed-effects-models.qmd`),
logistic section.

::: {.callout-note}
## Dataset: `lmd.rda` (placeholder)

I've written this section assuming `lmd.rda` has a binary outcome
variable and at least two predictors + a grouping variable (speaker or
item). If your actual data file has different columns, swap the column
names in the demo and exercise code before Day 3.
:::

### 3.1 Intro (15 min)

Key points:

- **When to go logistic.** Your outcome is binary: present/absent,
  used/not-used, correct/incorrect, yes/no. A linear model is wrong
  for binary outcomes — predictions can fall outside [0, 1] and
  residuals are not normal.
- **The link function.** Logistic regression models the LOG-ODDS of
  the outcome, not the probability directly. `glm(y ~ x,
  family = binomial)` does the maths.
- **Interpreting coefficients.** A log-odds of 0.5 means… nothing
  intuitive. Exponentiate to get odds ratios: `exp(0.5) = 1.65` →
  "odds of the outcome are 1.65 times higher per unit of x".
- **The mixed version.** Same random-effects idea as linear MEM, but
  with `glmer()` and `family = binomial`. Random intercepts and
  slopes for Speaker/Item/etc. are standard.
- **A caution.** Logistic MEMs are more fragile than linear MEMs.
  They need more data, converge less reliably, and warn more. We'll
  use the simplest possible structure that answers the question.

### 3.2 Students try (15 min)

> Load the data (swap `lmd.rda` for whatever file you have):
>
> ```r
> library(lme4)
> library(lmerTest)
> library(here)
>
> lmd <- readRDS(here::here("data", "lmd.rda"))
> head(lmd)
> glimpse(lmd)
>
> # Check: what's the binary outcome?
> # (If `Outcome` isn't the actual column name, use whichever is)
> table(lmd$Outcome)
> ```
>
> Fit the simplest possible logistic MEM:
>
> ```r
> m_log1 <- glmer(Outcome ~ Predictor1 + (1 | Speaker),
>                 data = lmd,
>                 family = binomial)
> summary(m_log1)
> ```
>
> (Swap column names to match your data.)

### 3.3 Demo (25 min)

```{r demo-3-3, eval=TRUE}
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(sjPlot)
library(performance)

# Fit the model
m_log <- glmer(Outcome ~ Predictor1 + Predictor2 + (1 | Speaker),
               data = lmd,
               family = binomial)
summary(m_log)

# The log-odds coefficients mean nothing intuitive
# Exponentiate to odds ratios
exp(fixef(m_log))

# Or get odds ratios + CIs with sjPlot
sjPlot::tab_model(m_log)

# Visualise predicted probabilities for one predictor
sjPlot::plot_model(m_log, type = "pred", terms = "Predictor1")

# Diagnostics
performance::check_model(m_log)

# Model fit metrics
performance::r2(m_log)
```

Talking points:

- The intercept in log-odds space is almost never interpretable
  directly — always visualise or exponentiate
- `sjPlot::plot_model(type = "pred")` is the single most useful
  function for communicating logistic regression results
- Marginal R² tells you how much variance the fixed effects explain;
  conditional R² adds the random effects
- Convergence warnings are common. If you get one, try:
  (a) simpler random structure, (b) centre numeric predictors,
  (c) a different optimizer: `control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")`

### 3.4 Exercise (20 min)

> **Task.** Using the dataset you have:
>
> 1. Fit a logistic MEM with your binary outcome, one fixed predictor,
>    and one random intercept
> 2. Report the odds ratio for your predictor with its 95% CI
> 3. Produce a predicted-probability plot with `sjPlot::plot_model()`
> 4. Save the plot
>
> **Stretch:** add a second fixed predictor and compare the two models
> with `anova()` — does the second predictor justify its complexity?

## 14:30–15:30 · §4. Conditional inference trees (60 min)

**Aim.** Every student fits a conditional inference tree, interprets
the plot, and produces a publication-quality version with `ggparty`.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 8, CIT subsection.

::: {.callout-note}
## This is a subsection of Ch 8, not a separate chapter

As agreed: CITs sit at the end of Ch 8 as a follow-up to the regression
material. The teaching framing: "we've done regression. Here's a
non-parametric alternative that's good at finding interactions."
:::

### 4.1 Intro (15 min)

Key points:

- **The problem CITs solve.** Regression tells you direction and
  magnitude (coefficient + CI). It is weaker at detecting complex
  interactions. If you suspect a three-way interaction between Age,
  Gender, and Status, a regression model requires you to specify
  it; a tree finds it.
- **How CITs work.** The algorithm splits your data into
  increasingly homogeneous subgroups. At each node, it asks: is
  any predictor significantly associated with the outcome? If yes,
  split on the strongest one. If no, stop.
- **CITs vs regression — complementary, not competitors.**
  Regression gives direction, magnitude, significance for specific
  predictors. CITs give a visual summary of how predictors interact.
  Use both.
- **CITs vs CARTs** (older-style decision trees). CITs use significance
  tests to decide when to stop splitting — more principled, less
  prone to overfitting.
- **What CITs don't give you.** Direction (which category is more
  likely) is readable from the leaf-node bar charts but not
  quantified. Effect sizes are visual. For publication, pair with
  a regression model.

### 4.2 Students try (10 min)

> Load the LADAL discourse-*like* dataset:
>
> ```r
> library(partykit)
> library(dplyr)
> library(here)
>
> citdata <- read.delim(here::here("data", "treedata.txt"),
>                       header = TRUE, sep = "\t") |>
>   dplyr::mutate_if(is.character, factor)
>
> head(citdata)
> str(citdata)
> ```
>
> Fit the simplest possible CIT:
>
> ```r
> set.seed(111)
> ct1 <- ctree(LikeUser ~ Age + Gender + Status, data = citdata)
> plot(ct1)
> ```
>
> Can you read the plot? What's at the top (root)? What do the leaf
> bars show?

### 4.3 Demo (20 min)

```{r demo-4-3, eval=TRUE}
library(partykit)
library(ggparty)
library(ggplot2)

# Basic fit
set.seed(111)
ct1 <- ctree(LikeUser ~ Age + Gender + Status, data = citdata)
plot(ct1)

# What's in the tree?
nodeids(ct1)                     # all nodes
nodeids(ct1, terminal = TRUE)    # leaf nodes

# Extract p-values at internal nodes
pvals <- unlist(nodeapply(ct1, ids = nodeids(ct1),
                          FUN = function(n) info_node(n)$p.value))
pvals[!is.na(pvals)]

# Predicted classes and probabilities
predict(ct1, type = "response") |> head()
predict(ct1, type = "prob") |> head()

# Publication-quality version with ggparty
ggparty(ct1) +
  geom_edge() +
  geom_edge_label() +
  geom_node_label(
    line_list = list(
      aes(label = splitvar),
      aes(label = paste0("N=", nodesize, ", p=",
                         format.pval(info_node(node)$p.value, digits = 2))),
      size = 10
    ),
    ids = "inner"
  ) +
  geom_node_label(
    aes(label = paste0("Node ", id, "\nN=", nodesize)),
    ids = "terminal"
  ) +
  geom_node_plot(
    gglist = list(
      geom_bar(aes(x = "", fill = LikeUser),
               position = position_fill(), color = "black"),
      theme_minimal(),
      scale_fill_manual(values = c("gray50", "gray80"), guide = "none"),
      scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1)),
      xlab(""),
      ylab("Probability")
    ),
    shared_axis_labels = TRUE
  ) +
  labs(title = "CIT: discourse 'like' usage",
       subtitle = "Predictors: Age, Gender, Status")
```

Talking points:

- The root node is the strongest-associated predictor (lowest p-value
  at that stage of splitting). In this data, likely Age
- Leaf bars show the distribution of the outcome in that subgroup —
  taller bar = predicted class
- `ggparty` is substantially nicer than `plot()` for publication but
  takes more code — the version above is a reasonable template
- `set.seed()` matters: CITs can be sensitive to tie-breaking in
  permutation tests. Always set a seed for reproducibility.

### 4.4 Exercise (15 min)

> **Task.** Using `citdata`:
>
> 1. Fit a CIT with all three predictors
> 2. Produce a `ggparty` version with proper labels
> 3. Save the plot to `figures/`
> 4. Write 2–3 sentences interpreting the tree in plain English — what
>    does it tell you about who uses discourse *like*?
> 5. Commit the plot and the interpretation
>
> **Stretch:** try `alpha = 0.01` in `ctree_control()` — how does the
> stricter threshold change the tree?

### 15:50–16:30 · Prüfungsleistung Q&A (40 min)

Open floor. Likely questions to prepare for:

- "What counts as a method from the seminar?" — any of: dplyr-based
  cleaning, ggplot2 visualisation, concordancing, frequency analysis,
  collocation, keyword analysis, mixed-effects, CIT. Pick one, apply
  it to a worked example.
- "Can I use my own data?" — yes, strongly encouraged
- "What data if I don't have any?" — point at Project Gutenberg,
  ICE corpora if licensed, the course data
- "How long should it be?" — refer to the README page counts (8–12
  for WP 33.1, 5–8 for others; 15–20 for Hausarbeit)
- "What if my Quarto doesn't render?" — Day 4 covers this; bring
  specific errors to Day 4 for debugging
- "When do I need to decide on a topic?" — soon, but you have until
  31 March 2027 to submit
- "Can I collaborate with another student?" — depends on your
  Prüfungsordnung; verify with your Prüfungsamt (standard disclaimer)

End the day explicitly: "See you tomorrow for Day 4 — bring your
laptop and your questions."
